title: Building Cache Middleware for Express
description: Create reusable Express middleware to cache GET responses automatically using Redis.

data.text: Middleware is Express.js's most powerful abstraction: it intercepts requests before they reach route handlers and responses before they reach the client. A cache middleware wraps this pattern by checking Redis on inbound requests and short-circuiting the response on a hit. Well-written cache middleware is reusable, declarative, and keeps caching logic completely separate from business logic.

Express middleware is a function with the signature `(req, res, next) => void`. For caching, the middleware runs before the route handler. It reads the request URL and optionally the query string to build a cache key. If the key exists in Redis, it sends the cached response and skips `next()`. Otherwise, it calls `next()` and intercepts `res.json` to store the response body on completion.

data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as Cache Middleware
    participant R as Redis
    participant H as Route Handler

    C->>M: GET /api/products/42
    M->>R: GET product:42
    alt Cache Hit
        R-->>M: JSON body
        M-->>C: 200 JSON (from cache)
    else Cache Miss
        M->>H: next()
        H-->>M: res.json(data)
        M->>R: SET product:42 EX 300
        M-->>C: 200 JSON
    end
data.caption: Cache middleware sequence diagram

data.text: The implementation below intercepts the response end event to capture the body. It builds cache keys from the request method, original URL, and any query parameters. Only GET requests are cached; mutations (POST, PUT, DELETE) are passed through without caching.

data.title: cacheMiddleware implementation
Use X-Cache Header
data.text: Always return an X-Cache header (HIT or MISS). This lets you verify caching behavior in the browser or API client and debug production issues without Redis access.

Not every route benefits from caching. Public read-only endpoints (product catalogs, FAQ pages) are perfect candidates. User-specific or mutation routes should bypass the cache. Use route-level middleware application to avoid accidental data leakage between users.

data.title: Applying middleware to specific routes
data.content: Use the middleware factory on routes that benefit from caching.

data.text: When your application mutates data, the corresponding cache entry becomes stale. The simplest approach is to delete the relevant keys immediately after the mutation succeeds. For dependent resources (e.g., a product list after a product update), use a cache tag or pattern-based deletion with SCAN + DEL or Redis keyspace notifications.

data.title: Invalidating cache after a mutation
data.content: Delete related cache keys after updating a product.

data.title: Always Invalidate After Writes
data.text: A cache that is never invalidated serves stale data to clients. The standard rule: if you write to the database, delete the cache. If you write to the cache, ensure the database update succeeds first.

data.title: Middleware design rules
items: Never cache responses with Set-Cookie headers
Use a consistent namespace prefix in cache keys

items.question: Should I apply the middleware globally?
items.answer: Prefer route-level application. A global cache middleware can accidentally cache private user data or error responses if a handler throws.

items.question: How do I handle cache warmup?
items.answer: On deployment, issue GET requests to critical routes or use a warmup script that SETs known keys with full TTLs so the first real users see instant responses.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Cache middleware intercepts GET requests, short-circuits hits, and stores misses.
Always separate public and private routes when applying caching middleware.
Pair cache writes with DELETE calls on mutations to prevent stale data.
Use the X-Cache header to make caching behavior visible to developers and operators.
